Tool application · Microsoft Power BI

Power BI can show an HR team where staff turnover is costing money, and where to act first

16.1%overall attrition237 of 1,470 employees
30.5%with overtimevs 10.4% without
29.8%in first 2 yearsvs 8.1% after 11+ years
£30,614to replace one employeeUK average · Oxford Economics, 2014

1Introduction

Staff turnover is expensive: Oxford Economics estimated that replacing one UK employee costs £30,614 on average. Yet many HR teams cannot say where or why people leave. This entry shows how Microsoft Power BI could turn HR data into evidence for retention decisions.

2Application

I chose Power BI over Excel and Tableau because it connects directly to the spreadsheets and HR exports most teams already use, Power BI Desktop is free, and sharing costs $14 per user per month on the Pro plan. Row-level security also lets managers see only their own team's data, which matters for sensitive HR records.

I designed a dashboard for the IBM HR Analytics dataset (1,470 fictional employees). Power Query would clean the data, a DAX measure would calculate the attrition rate, and KPI cards, charts and slicers would let managers explore it (Figure 1). The dataset shows that overtime workers leave at 30.5% compared with 10.4%, attrition is 29.8% in the first two years, and Sales Representatives are the highest-risk role.

3Critical evaluation

The business value lies in targeting. If the company cut attrition by just two percentage points, about 29 fewer people would leave, a potential saving of roughly £0.9 million at the Oxford Economics average, against a licence cost of under $1,700 a year for ten Pro users (Figure 3).

However, the dashboard is descriptive: it shows that overtime and leaving occur together, not that one causes the other. Its insights are only as good as the data, and this dataset is fictional. Employee records are personal data under UK GDPR, so access must be restricted and figures aggregated. There is also an ethical risk that managers use the same data to label individuals as "flight risks" without their knowledge.

4Conclusion

Power BI creates value not by producing charts but by helping managers spend retention budgets where turnover is highest, such as Sales and new starters. Under the right conditions (good data quality, privacy controls and managers who act on the evidence), it offers a low-cost, high-return way to make better people decisions.

02
Case analysis · Amazon, 2014–2018

Amazon's recruiting AI shows that a model can work perfectly and still fail the business

1Introduction

Recruitment is one of the most common uses of AI in HR, and one of the most sensitive. This entry analyses Amazon's experimental CV-screening tool, which was abandoned after it learned to favour men, and asks what businesses can learn from it (Reuters, 2018).

2Analysis: what happened and why

From 2014, an Amazon team in Edinburgh built a machine-learning tool that rated applicants from one to five stars. It was trained on CVs submitted over the previous ten years, most of which came from men. By 2015, Amazon realised the system was not rating technical candidates in a gender-neutral way: it penalised CVs containing the word "women's" and downgraded graduates of two all-women's colleges.

The problem occurred because the model treated past hiring decisions as a definition of a good candidate. Engineers removed the obvious terms, but could not guarantee the system would not find other proxies, such as hobbies or wording. The project was abandoned in early 2017, and Amazon said recruiters never relied on its rankings.

3Critical evaluation

For the business, the tool wasted years of specialist effort and, if used, would have shrunk the talent pool in a sector short of engineers. The 2018 coverage turned an internal experiment into a global story about "sexist AI", damaging Amazon's employer brand. In the UK, a similar tool could lead to indirect discrimination claims under the Equality Act 2010.

Ethically, the case raises three issues: fairness (equally skilled women scored lower), transparency (applicants could not challenge their score) and accountability (who answers for an algorithm's decision?). To its credit, Amazon's own testing found the problem.

What Amazon should have done differently: defined fairness first, audited the training data, tested scores by gender before use, kept human review with a right to appeal, and monitored outcomes (Figure 6).

4Conclusion

The model did exactly what it was trained to do, which is why it failed. The lesson for any business is that responsible AI is a management process, not a technical fix: fairness must be designed in, tested and owned by people before an algorithm touches real candidates.

What should have happened: five checkpoints

  1. Define fairnessAgree what "fair" means and who is accountable before building.
  2. Audit the dataCheck training data for gender imbalance and proxies.
  3. Test outcomes by groupCompare scores for men and women before any real use.
  4. Human review and appealA recruiter decides; applicants can ask for a review.
  5. Monitor after launchTrack shortlist rates by group and switch off if bias appears.

Figure 6. Framework of the checkpoints Amazon's project lacked. Step 3 is where Amazon found the bias, but only after the tool had been built.

One word, a different score

03
Digital strategy insight · AI-driven business transformation

AI is turning recruitment from an admin task into a strategic capability, but only well-governed firms will keep the advantage

72%of HR professionals use AI weekly2025, up from 58% · HireVue
91%of US HR leaders use AI in hiringPaylocity, 1,000+ leaders
100,000interview hours saved a yearUnilever · The Guardian, 2019
~300ICO recommendations to AI hiring tool providersUK audit, November 2024

1Introduction

AI is now an everyday recruitment tool: weekly use among HR professionals rose from 58% in 2024 to 72% in 2025 (HireVue, 2025). This entry assesses how AI-driven recruitment, including generative AI, could transform talent strategy, and under what conditions the benefits outweigh the risks.

2Application: how the trend changes strategy

Unilever shows the shift. For its graduate programme, which attracts around 250,000 applicants for 800 places, it replaced CV sifting with online games and AI-analysed video interviews. Unilever said this saves about 100,000 hours of interviewing time and roughly $1 million a year (The Guardian, 2019), while its vendor reported faster hiring and more diverse hires (HireVue, n.d.).

Generative AI extends this by drafting job adverts, personalising messages to candidates and summarising interviews (Figure 9). Strategically, recruitment moves from an administrative cost to a data-driven capability: firms can reach wider and more diverse talent pools, hire faster than competitors, make decisions from evidence rather than instinct, and redeploy recruiters to relationship-building and final assessment.

3Critical evaluation

The benefits depend on five conditions (Figure 8). Implementation costs go beyond licences to integration, training and bias audits. Data security and privacy are real concerns: a UK ICO audit found some tools collected more personal data than needed, kept it indefinitely or let recruiters filter out people with protected characteristics. Workforce implications include fewer administrative roles and a need for AI skills in HR.

Dependence on technology creates legal risk: in Mobley v. Workday, a US court let applicants over 40 pursue a collective age-discrimination claim against an AI screening provider. Finally, long-term competitive advantage is limited, because rivals can buy the same tools; the lasting advantage comes from trusted governance and a strong employer brand.

4Conclusion

AI-driven recruitment can transform talent strategy, but it benefits large-volume employers most, and only when they keep humans accountable. I recommend a staged approach: adopt AI first for low-risk support tasks, add screening only with audits and transparency, and treat governance as the source of competitive advantage.

Strategic assessment: five factors a manager must weigh

Implementation costsSavings at scale, e.g. Unilever's ~$1m a yearIntegration, training and audit costsMedium
Data security and privacyConsistent, documented processesExcess data kept indefinitely (ICO, 2024)High risk

Recommendation: a staged strategy

  1. Assist

    Adopt AI first for drafting, scheduling and candidate communication.

  2. Screen with safeguards

    Use AI screening only with bias audits, transparency to candidates and a named human decision-maker.

  3. Govern for advantage

    Follow ICO guidance and prepare for EU AI Act duties from December 2027, building trust that rivals cannot buy.

04
Reflective summary

I began seeing AI as a way to remove human judgement. I finish seeing it as a way to strengthen it.

1Learning development

Looking back over this module and the three entries in this portfolio, I can see clearly how my thinking about AI has changed, from excitement about speed and efficiency to a more balanced view of what AI can and cannot do for people and organisations.

Before this module, I saw AI mainly as a tool for automating tasks, such as screening hundreds of CVs in seconds. I assumed that being data-driven meant being objective. Designing the attrition dashboard changed this view. Every chart depended on my choices: which data to include, how to group tenure and age, and which questions to ask. The same data could support very different decisions depending on who was reading it.

The Amazon case made this concrete. Nothing in the algorithm was "broken"; it faithfully reproduced past patterns. Researching Unilever then showed me the other side: AI can transform a whole business process and save time and money when it is designed carefully. I now understand digital management as the governance of data, people and processes around a tool, not just the choice of tool.

2Ethical awareness

The most important lesson for me is that bias in AI is harder to see, and so harder to challenge, than bias in one person. A biased manager affects a few candidates; a biased algorithm can affect thousands, quietly and at scale. Rejected applicants rarely know why, which weakens their ability to contest decisions.

I also learned how closely fairness is linked to privacy. The ICO audit showed that some recruitment tools collected far more personal data than they needed and kept it indefinitely. Before, I thought of privacy as a legal box to tick; now I see it as part of treating people with respect. I also realised that "human in the loop" can become a box-ticking exercise: if people approve whatever the system recommends, oversight exists on paper only.

3Professional development

My background is in education, where I worked as a primary teacher and librarian. In both roles I saw how much decisions about people depend on context and care, which is exactly what an algorithm can miss. In my future career, whether in education or HR, I will apply three principles: question the data first, keep humans accountable for decisions, and monitor outcomes for different groups, not just overall accuracy.

Practically, I now have skills I can use straight away: analysing HR data and designing dashboards, evaluating AI tools against ethical and legal criteria, and explaining both the benefits and risks to non-technical colleagues. This module has changed my view of AI from a threat or a shortcut into a tool that, used responsibly, can help organisations make fairer and better decisions.

The question I will keep asking in every role is not only "can AI do this?" but "should it, for whom, and under what conditions?" That question is the most valuable thing I am taking away from this module.

Three principles I will take into my career

Question the data first

Ask what historical data a model learned from, and whose experience it leaves out.

Keep humans accountable

AI can shortlist, summarise or flag patterns; final decisions rest with a trained person who can explain them.

Monitor outcomes, not just accuracy

Track results by gender, age and ethnicity, using dashboards like the one in Entry 1, to catch unfair patterns early.
